source.title: A Spectral Theory of Grokking: Weight Decay induces Feature Learning
source.authors: Lenz Pracher; Pascal de Jong; Oskar Lieshaus; Alan Jeffares; S. Rulands

record.tranche_reason: The study tests delayed generalization and post-fit feature evolution on modular addition using NTK measurements, theoretical reductions, and optimizer sweeps rather than reproducing the original studies' methods.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites results from other work on grokking and related mechanisms; those cited results are not recorded as rows. The paper's own results include theoretical derivations, modular-addition experiments, optimizer-grid outcomes, and a temporary NTK-alignment intervention.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own modular-addition experiments (MLP and Transformer optimizer grids, NTK spectral diagnostics, a paired NTK-alignment intervention). These bear directly on delayed generalization and its gradual mechanism, using NTK and optimizer-plane methods rather than the original circuit analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that coupled weight decay leaves a post-fit residual that drives task-aligned NTK growth, explaining delayed generalization and its phase structure in the (η, λW) plane. The MLP recovers the predicted phase geometry and (ηλW)^-1 timing, and a Transformer shows similar macroscopic behaviour. They also stress that (ηλW)^-1 timing alone does not distinguish feature learning from fixed-feature delays; the NTK measurements and intervention are meant to do that.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies residual-dependent NTK evolution, optimizer-plane sweeps, and a temporary NTK-alignment intervention; it does not reproduce the original studies' mechanistic circuit analysis or original grokking experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary across learning rate and weight decay, with reported memorization, grokking, forgetting/non-fitting, and instability regions. The study also uses different accuracy-crossing thresholds for the MLP and Transformer timing analyses.

fits_no_version.finding: The grokking delay scales as (ηλW)^-1 in both MLP and Transformer. The calibrated boundary has log-log slope −0.9043 vs the empirical −1.1681.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The grokking delay is set by the per-update weight-decay scale ηλW (shared with fixed-feature accounts).

record.code_released: The paper says the code will be made publicly available upon publication; the artifact URL is not supplied in the text.
record.problems: The main optimizer sweeps use a fixed model initialization seed at each grid point. The experiments study modular addition rather than a range of datasets, do not vary training-set size, and use 90% grokking criteria. The fitted MLP boundary parameters are inferred from the optimizer boundary rather than measured NTK trajectories; the scalar theory relies on one-mode and adiabatic assumptions.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size (split size is fixed); a near-perfect endpoint (grokking is defined at 90%); onset from chance level.
Formation of a specific mechanistic circuit; later removal of memorizing components; whether continuous measures anticipate the accuracy jump.
Non-algorithmic data (images, text, molecules); initialization scale as the control. Only weight decay and learning rate are varied.
All; there is no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
An efficiency comparison between generalizing and memorizing circuits; a critical dataset size; ungrokking below it.
All; learned algorithms are not compared across runs, and the grids use one init seed.
No explicit control experiment. Only the incidental fact that runs use full-batch SGD and MSE bears on it; floating-point precision is not reported.

missing.what: Representative trajectories: the grokking run first reaches 90% held-out at update 8,300. The forgetting run peaks at 0.948 training accuracy and ends at 0.204. This is direct evidence of the delay.
Optimizer and loss configuration (full-batch SGD, no momentum, MSE loss) under which grokking occurs. This bears on artifact accounts.
Held-out accuracy timing for the modulo-97 diagnostic run relative to the NTK organization (Fig 2b), with no numeric crossing stated.
Theoretical argument that smooth mode growth yields a sharp accuracy jump via a narrow distribution of margin thresholds.
Boundary slope diagnostics: empirical −1.1681 vs calibrated −0.9043.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Several reader choices were corrected. The R1/R2 theory rows are no longer labelled 'observed'. The 90% criterion is moved from limits_scope to untested. V5 links are removed from the timing rows. The V3 and V7 verdicts are inferential: V3 rests on weight decay acting as a regime control on algorithmic data only. V7 rests on grokking appearing with plain SGD and MSE, which the paper does not present as an artifact test; researchers may weigh these more lightly. Every grid cell uses init seed 0, so there is no seed variability for the phase maps.

versions.untested_parts: It does not vary training-set size, so it does not test whether smaller training sets require more optimization. Its experimental grokking criteria use 90% accuracy rather than establishing near-perfect accuracy.

It tracks task-aligned NTK/Fourier organization and residual-driven mode growth, not the formation of the specific mechanistic circuit or removal of memorizing components. It does not test whether mechanistic progress measures anticipate the accuracy jump.
The experiments use modular addition, not non-algorithmic data. Initialization scale and weight norm are not varied; the paper varies learning rate and weight decay.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.

The paper studies weight-decay-dependent feature growth, timing, and cutoffs, but does not test an efficiency comparison between generalizing and memorizing circuits or vary dataset size to identify a critical dataset size.
The study does not identify and compare learned algorithms across runs; its optimizer grids use a fixed initialization seed at each grid point.
It does not test whether optimizer or numerical artifacts produce the delay, or whether controlling them removes it.

rows.subject: D-homogeneous network (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Derives the fixed-NTK residual dynamics under coupled L2 weight decay and squared loss.
rows.measure: Equilibrium residual fraction in target-projected NTK eigendirections
rows.value: The derived residual coefficient is proportional to DλnormW/(Λj + DλnormW); for a fixed target projection, weaker NTK eigenmodes retain a larger residual fraction.
rows.note: Analytical result; it does not depend on modular addition, though the later spectral reduction uses that task's Fourier structure.
rows.check: Theorem 1 is an analytical derivation of the equilibrium residual under a fixed NTK. It measures no delay, circuit or generalization behaviour, so it bears on no version. It is the study's own theory, not a result row.

rows.subject: One-hidden-layer two-homogeneous ReLU MLP (reduced theoretical mode)
rows.operation_detail: Projects the neural tangent hierarchy onto one task-aligned mode and derives its residual–NTK dynamics.

conditions.value: one task-aligned direction with weak mixing

rows.measure: Predicted post-fit task-mode strength and transition timescale
rows.value: Residual-driven NTK growth competes with decay; the derived slow update scale is (ηλW)−1, and a sufficiently high decay can make a selected generalization threshold unreachable.
rows.note: This is a theoretical prediction conditional on the stated one-mode, positive-coupling, and adiabatic assumptions.
rows.check: Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 are derivations under one-mode, constant-coupling and adiabatic assumptions. They predict decay-controlled slow growth and a high-decay cutoff but measure nothing. Marking them 'observed' overstates them; treat them as argument only.

rows.subject: Bias-free 194 → 256 → 97 ReLU MLP
rows.operation_detail: Tracks a normalized label-space NTK projected through true-label outputs during modular-addition training.
rows.measure: Periodic/Fourier-like structure in normalized label-space NTK
rows.value: Periodic structure strengthens between updates 3,000 and 20,000; leading eigenvectors develop Fourier-like standing-wave profiles after training accuracy is already high.
rows.note: The paper describes the kernel organization and its timing in text; the plots provide the displayed trajectories.
rows.check: Fourier-like NTK structure develops gradually after training fit, which fits V2's gradual-mechanism part. It is one seed, tracks NTK rather than a circuit, and does not show memorizing components removed. It does not test whether the measure anticipates the held-out jump; no held-out timing numbers are given.

rows.subject: Bias-free 46 → 256 → 23 ReLU MLP
rows.operation_detail: Sweeps learning rate and weight decay over an optimizer grid and classifies final training/held-out outcomes.
rows.measure: Memorizing, grokking, forgetting, and non-fitting outcome regions in the learning-rate/weight-decay plane
rows.value: The grid contains a weak-decay memorization region, an intermediate grokking band, and non-fitting or other failure regions; increasing decay eventually prevents mode reachability or training fit.
rows.note: Grokking is operationalized using a 90% threshold. The grid is reported as a whole, with one fixed initialization seed.
rows.check: These are final-state classifications at a 90% criterion with one init seed per cell. Delayed generalization itself is shown only in Fig 7 and Fig 3b. V3 link: weight decay (a weight-norm control) switches memorization vs grokking within a fixed budget on algorithmic data only. V5 link: weak decay memorizes and intermediate decay groks; critical dataset size and ungrokking are not tested.

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine for temporal grokking, delay switches, and circuit efficiency. The grid measures final training/held-out outcomes after 24,000 updates using a 90% threshold; temporal evidence is reported separately in Figures 3b and 7.
source_check.problem: Final-state classifications alone cannot establish the linked versions' temporal or circuit-efficiency effects.

rows.subject: Bias-free 46 → 256 → 23 ReLU MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compares first held-out 10% accuracy crossing times with inverse learning-rate/weight-decay product.

conditions.value: runs that eventually reach at least 90% held-out accuracy

rows.value: Observed crossing times follow the predicted scaling across the grokking region.
rows.note: The fitted scalar-boundary parameters are inferred from the optimizer boundary, not direct measurements of NTK strength.
rows.check: Removed the V5 link. The (ηλW)^-1 timing law is about delay set by optimizer hyperparameters, not an efficiency comparison. The authors note that fixed-feature models give the same scaling. The baseline is the predicted scaling, not a control.

rows.subject: One-block pre-norm Transformer
rows.size_stated: dmodel = 32; four attention heads; feed-forward width 64
rows.operation_detail: Sweeps learning rate and weight decay and classifies final training/held-out outcomes.
rows.measure: Memorizing, grokking, and failure regions in the learning-rate/weight-decay plane
rows.value: The paper reports a weak-decay memorization region, an intermediate grokking band, and failure at stronger decay or large learning rate.
rows.note: This tests a non-homogeneous architecture, but still on modular addition; the 90% criterion is not near-perfect accuracy.
rows.check: Same caveats as R4: final-state 90% classification, one seed, modular addition only. Added a V3 link because weight decay switches outcomes in a non-homogeneous model.

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine for delayed generalization and temporal delay switches. Figure 4a classifies final outcomes after 60,000 updates using a 90% threshold; Figure 4b separately measures first held-out 80% crossings.
source_check.problem: The final-state grid does not itself demonstrate train/test timing separation or switches in that separation.

rows.subject: One-block pre-norm Transformer
rows.size_stated: dmodel = 32; four attention heads; feed-forward width 64
rows.operation_detail: Compares first held-out 80% crossing times with inverse learning-rate/weight-decay product.

conditions.value: runs that eventually reach the 90% grokking criterion

rows.value: The first held-out 80% crossing follows the same linear scaling; the grokking cohort's median ηλW s80 is 0.920.
rows.note: The paper uses the 80% crossing because early 10% crossings can be reversible.
rows.check: Removed the V5 link for the same reason as R5. The 80% crossing threshold differs from the MLP's 10%, so timing is not directly comparable across architectures.

rows.subject: Paired bias-free 194 → 256 → 97 ReLU students
rows.operation_detail: Adds a temporary penalty matching the student label NTK to a teacher label NTK for updates 0–2,999, then removes it.
rows.value: Intervention: 13,527.5 updates; reported mean speedup 1.498 and median paired speedup 1.489.
rows.uncertainty: One sample standard deviation across 40 paired seeds is shown in Figure 6; numerical error-bar values are not stated.
rows.note: Both members of each pair share data and initialization and use the same objective after the intervention ends. The paper says the intervention changes several Fourier components, so it does not isolate the scalar one-mode mechanism.
rows.check: This is an intervention compared against a paired baseline. It shows that early task-aligned NTK structure advances the later held-out crossing (20,200 to 13,527.5 updates), consistent with a gradual underlying build-up. It does not measure a circuit or progress measure anticipating the jump. The authors say the kernel match changes several Fourier components, so it is indirect.

relationships.condition: Modulo-23 bias-free MLP and one-block Transformer, full-batch SGD with MSE, 90% criterion
relationships.reason: Both grids show a memorization region and a grokking band, and held-out crossings lag fit and scale with (ηλW)^-1 (R4–R7). Fig 7 shows a run reaching 90% held-out only at update 8,300, from text.
relationships.display_finding: Both model grids exhibited memorization and grokking regions, with held-out threshold crossings lagging training fit and scaling as (ηλW)^-1, including a run reaching 90% at update 8,300.

relationships.condition: Gradual-formation part only; modulo-97 bias-free MLP, single seed for diagnostic, 40 paired seeds for intervention
relationships.reason: NTK Fourier structure strengthens gradually after fit (R3), and early alignment speeds held-out generalization about 1.5× (R8). Circuit formation, memorization removal and anticipation are not tested.
relationships.display_finding: NTK Fourier structure strengthens gradually after fitting, and early alignment accelerates held-out generalization by approximately 1.5× without testing circuit formation, memorization removal, or anticipation.

source_check.reason: R3 shows post-fit Fourier-like NTK organization; R8 shows earlier held-out generalization after early alignment. This supports the specified gradual-formation component; circuit identification and memorization removal remain untested.

relationships.condition: Regime-control part only, on algorithmic data: weight decay and learning rate in modulo-23 MLP and Transformer under a fixed update budget
relationships.reason: Weak decay leaves runs memorizing, while intermediate decay produces grokking in both architectures (R4, R6). This fits the lazy-to-rich framing, but laziness is not measured in the grid.
relationships.display_finding: Weak weight decay left both architectures memorizing, whereas intermediate decay enabled generalization within the fixed training budget.

relationships.condition: Weight-decay part only; modulo-23 MLP grid
relationships.reason: Generalization within budget requires sufficient weight decay, with memorization at weak decay (R4). The efficiency, critical-dataset-size and ungrokking predictions are untested.

source_check.reason: R4 shows weight-decay dependence of final outcomes but does not measure comparative circuit efficiency or low-norm selection between memorizing and generalizing circuits. Critical dataset size and ungrokking are untested.

relationships.condition: Full-batch SGD without momentum; MSE on logits (MLP) or softmax probabilities (Transformer)
relationships.reason: Grokking occurs without adaptive optimizers or cross-entropy softmax (R4, R6; Appendix G.2–G.3 configs). This is a design choice the paper does not frame as an artifact control, so the evidence is from the text.
relationships.display_finding: Grokking occurred without adaptive optimizers or cross-entropy, although the training setup was not presented as a controlled test of numerical artifacts.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Full-batch SGD without momentum; MSE on logits (MLP) or softmax probabilities (Transformer)
source_check.reason: The SGD/MSE configurations provide counterexamples to necessity of adaptive optimization; the MLP also avoids softmax computation. The Transformer retains softmax. This challenges those specific artifact explanations, without constituting a comprehensive numerical-control ablation.

relation.reason: The paper reports its own empirical and theoretical results bearing directly on grokking.

tranche.reason: Own modular-addition experiments test delayed generalization and post-fit feature development using NTK diagnostics, optimizer grids, and an alignment intervention.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased, including that inverse-product timing alone does not identify feature learning. The pack abbreviates several row values; all visible numerical claims match the text.

statements.correction: NTK alignment advances mean first 50% held-out crossing from 20,200 to 13,527.5 updates across 40 paired seeds; paired mean speedup 1.498; median 1.489. Code release promised upon publication; public artifact URL absent. Sources: Appendix F.2, Figure 6, reproducibility statement, Appendix G.
statements.problem: The NTK intervention claim is supported, but public code availability is overstated: the text promises release upon publication and leaves the artifact URL unfilled.
